newsitem.title: CHINA: China hails Clinton decision on trade status.
newsitem.headline: China hails Clinton decision on trade status.

text.p: Beijing said on Tuesday it welcomed a move by U.S. President Bill Clinton to renew China's favoured trading status as a wise decision but urged Washington to grant the trade concessions permanently.
"We welcome President Clinton's announcement to extend Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status for China," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a regular news briefing.

Clinton told U.S. businessmen on Monday that he planned to renew most favoured nation trade status for China for another year, firing the opening shot in what is expected to be a new foreign policy battle with Congress.
Clinton said he had decided to accord China what amounted to normal trade tariff status for the next year despite disputes with Beijing on many issues, notably human rights.
"We think that this decision by President Clinton is a wise decision," Shen said.
However, he said the annual review of the trading status for China was not conducive to the normal and stable development of trade ties, and urged Washington to grant permanent MFN.
The Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation backed Clinton's move and called for a halt to the annual review system.

"(We) hope the U.S. can soon take measures to alter the current unreasonable and untimely method of annual reviews of MFN and permanently resolve the issue of MFN for China to ensure the smooth and stable development of trade relations," it said.
Shen fired a shot at the U.S. Congress, where opponents of trade concessions to China are expected to mount the fiercest congressional battle in years to overturn Clinton's decision.
"The U.S. Congress should not engage in unnecessary interference in MFN for China or cancel MFN," Shen said. "This is not in the interests of either side."
While supporters of the president's decision to renew MFN remain confident of victory, social conservatives, organised labour and other opponents are preparing for a fight.
The unusual coalition is blasting the move from both sides of the political spectrum, hitting China's policies on human rights, labour rights, religious rights, trade and abortion.

Opponents are also gathering strength from worries over the transfer of Hong Kong to China, as well as the controversy over charges that Beijing tried to sway U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
Asked about the link with Hong Kong, which is to revert to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, Shen said there was no reason to twin the issues.
MFN renewal should not hinge on the smooth transition of Hong Kong, he said.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said this year's decision would be closer than last year's 286-141 vote in the House to back Clinton on MFN. But advocates and even opponents expect the president's policy ultimately to survive.

MFN gives China the normal trade status the United States accords all but six nations: Afghanistan, Cuba, Laos, North Korea, Serbia and Vietnam. Iran, Iraq and Libya technically enjoy MFN status but are subject to separate trade embargoes.
The move to renew China's MFN status is an annual decision that every president has made since 1980.

Under the law, Clinton must formally inform Congress of his decision by June 3. To overturn the decision, the House of Representatives and the Senate have until August 31 to pass a joint resolution disapproving it.

The United States has an interest in maintaining normal trade relations. U.S. officials estimate that 170,000 U.S. jobs depend on exports to China and that ending MFN could cost U.S. consumers $600 million a year in higher prices for shoes, clothing and appliances.
